name: Max Factor makeup application device

card.summary: The Beauty Micrometer, an adjustable mask-like device from the early 1930s that mapped facial contours so makeup could soften or emphasise features.
card.note: A film-industry curiosity of 1932 that never became widely used; one example survives in a museum.

quick.overview:
The Beauty Micrometer, also called the Beauty Calibrator, was a device from the early 1930s credited to Max Factor Sr. It fitted around the head and face and measured contours so a makeup artist could see which features to enhance or tone down.

It was aimed mainly at the film industry, where close-ups magnify flaws, and its inventors also pictured beauty shops using it. It did not become popular, and only one example is believed to survive.
quick.how: Flexible metal strips aligned with facial features and screws allowed 325 adjustments, measuring to a thousandth of an inch. Its designers looked for matching nose and forehead heights and eyes spaced one eye-width apart.
quick.risks: The device is a historical item, not something sold today. Press coverage has compared it to an instrument of torture and to phrenology.

lead: The Beauty Micrometer, or Beauty Calibrator, was a mask-like measuring device from the early 1930s, completed in 1932, with Max Factor Sr. named as one of its inventors. [1] It was meant to identify facial features that makeup could enhance or subdue, so an artist could correct them. [1][2]
Flexible metal strips aligned with the face and screws allowed 325 adjustments, accurate to one thousandth of an inch. [1]
It never became widely used; one example is believed to survive, displayed at the Hollywood Entertainment Museum. [1]

chain: Reveals features that read as flaws on camera
Makeup applied to enhance or soften them
angle.text: The device was designed to guide where makeup should be placed by showing how a face departs from target proportions.

paras: The device fitted around the head and face; its inventors looked for matching nose and forehead heights and eyes one eye-width apart. [1] Max Factor, founder of the cosmetics company, specialised in film makeup and helped develop a device to measure facial contours and detect barely visible structural flaws that could stand out on camera. [2]

It never became popular. A 2009 auction fell well short of its $10,000-$20,000 estimate. The Guardian described it as looking like an instrument of torture and Wired compared it to a Clockwork Orange style device. [1]
